# Video SOPs: what they are and how to make one
URL: https://www.flexlore.com/guides/video-sop/
Language: en

A video SOP is a standard operating procedure shown as a short video of the real job, split into numbered steps with a line of text for each. To make one, film your best person doing one task on a phone, mark where each step starts, write the key values as text, add a short quiz and have it approved.

## What is a video SOP?

A video SOP is a standard operating procedure shown as a short video of the real job, split into numbered steps, with a line or two of text for each step. It answers the same question as a written SOP: how do we do this task here, every time. The difference is that people see the hands, the tools and the order instead of reading about them.

A good video SOP has four parts:

The video: one task, filmed where it happens, by the person who does it best.

Steps: the video cut into clips, one clip per step, so a new hire can replay only the step they are stuck on.

Text: a short instruction under each step with the details video cannot carry well: a temperature, a setting, a torque value, a warning.

A check: a few questions at the end that show whether the person understood the steps.

People also call these video work instructions, visual SOPs or video training procedures. On a production line the term is usually work instructions; in a kitchen or hotel it is more often SOP or standard. The format is the same.

## Video SOP vs written SOP: what is the difference?

Video shows how a task is done; text records exactly what must be true. Most teams need both, in one place, with video doing the showing and text holding the numbers and rules.

Question | Video SOP | Written SOP | 

Best at | Hand movements, order of work, what &quot;right&quot; looks like | Exact values, limits, sign-offs, policy wording | 

Who it suits | New hires, people working in a second language, visual learners | Auditors, supervisors, people checking a detail | 

Where it is used | On a phone, at the station, during the task | In a binder, a shared drive or printed at the station | 

Time to make | Film in minutes, then cut into steps and review | Write, format, review; often slower for physical tasks | 

Keeping it current | Re-film or replace only the step that changed | Edit text, reprint, collect old copies | 

Weak spot | Hard to search, easy to miss a number spoken once | Hard to picture, often skipped on the floor | 

If you already have written procedures, you do not need to throw them away. Use them as the script for what to film and keep the exact values as text on each step. Our SOP template is a useful starting structure.

## When does a video SOP work best, and when is written enough?

Use video when the hard part of the task is seeing it done. Stay with text when the hard part is remembering a rule or a number.

Video works best for

Physical tasks with a specific order: breaking down a slicer, threading a machine, making a bed to house standard.

Tasks where &quot;done right&quot; is visual: plating, a weld bead, a pallet wrap, a folded towel.

Safety steps where the movement matters: lockout, lifting, handling a hot fryer basket.

Teams with many languages or mixed reading levels.

Jobs one experienced person knows well and nobody has written down.

Written is often enough for

Policies and rules: dress code, break times, cash handling rules.

Short reference lists: allergen tables, supplier contacts, par levels.

Screen tasks with few steps, where a numbered list with screenshots does the job.

A quick test: if a new hire reads the written version and still asks someone to show them, that task needs a video.

## How to film a job on a phone: shot checklist

Film the person who does the job best, doing the real task at the real station, one task per video. A phone is enough. Use this checklist before you press record.

Before you film

Pick the right person. The one others go to with questions, not the most senior title.

Agree the steps first. Spend two minutes listing the steps out loud. That list becomes your step markers later.

One task per video. &quot;Closing the fryer station&quot; is one video. &quot;Closing the kitchen&quot; is a series.

Pick a quiet moment. Before opening, between rushes or during a planned changeover, not mid-service.

Clean up the station. Remove anything that should not be copied: a wrong tool, an open chemical bottle, a shortcut.

Ask permission. Tell the person and anyone in frame what the video is for and where it will be shown.

Framing and light

Hold the phone horizontal for wide stations, vertical if people will watch at a narrow station. Pick one and keep it.

Film from the worker&#39;s point of view, over the shoulder, so the viewer sees what they will see.

Get close for small details: dials, labels, the inside of a machine guard. Move the phone, do not zoom.

Keep light behind the camera, not behind the worker. Turn off a window glare if you can.

Lean on a shelf or use a small stand to keep the shot steady.

Sound

Ask the worker to say what they are doing and why, in plain words: &quot;I check the oil is at the line before I turn it on.&quot;

Film in a quieter moment or stand closer. Kitchens and lines are loud; key facts should also go in the step text.

Do not add music. It hides speech and adds nothing at the station.

Marking the steps while filming

Pause for a second between steps. Clean breaks make cutting easy.

Have the worker say the step number or name at the start: &quot;Step 3, empty the oil.&quot;

Show the finished result at the end of each step and of the task.

If something goes wrong, keep filming and redo the step. You will cut the mistake out.

## How to turn footage into steps, text and a short quiz

Cut the video at each step, write one or two lines per step, then add three to five questions that check the points people get wrong. Keep each step short enough to replay at the station.

Trim. Remove the start, the end and any waiting time.

Mark the steps. Set where each step starts and stops, using the pauses you left while filming. A step should be one action with one result.

Write the step text. Start with a verb: &quot;Turn the fryer off and wait until the oil is below the safe line.&quot; Put exact values here, not only in the speech.

Add on-screen labels where it matters. A temperature, a setting, an arrow at the right valve, a warning.

Write the quiz. Ask about the decisions, not trivia: &quot;What do you do before draining the oil?&quot; is better than &quot;What color is the bucket?&quot;. Three to five questions is usually enough for one task.

Read it as a new hire. Watch each step with the sound off. If it is unclear, the text needs work.

For tasks with tight tolerances or many settings, pair the video with a written work instruction that holds the full table of values.

## Who should review and approve a video SOP?

Two people: the expert who did the job checks that the steps are right, and the manager who owns the standard approves it for use. Nothing should go to the team until both are done.

Accuracy check (the expert): is every step shown, in the right order, with the right values?

Standard check (the owner): is this the way we want it done in every location, and does it match safety and hygiene rules that apply to you?

Clarity check (a new person): ask someone who has never done the task to watch it and say what they would do. Their questions show the gaps.

Record who approved it and when. Local rules decide what records you need for food safety or workplace safety, so check them. A written and approved procedure can support an audit, but it does not replace one.

If AI drafts any part of the text or quiz, treat it as a draft. A person who knows the job reads and approves every line.

## How to roll out video SOPs and keep them current

Start with the few tasks that cause the most mistakes or the most questions, assign them to the people who do those tasks, and check who watched and understood them. Then set a simple rule for updates.

Rollout

List the tasks new hires ask about most in their first week. Film those first.

Assign each video SOP by role and location, so a dishwasher does not wade through bar procedures.

Ask people to watch at the station, before they do the task for the first time.

Look at quiz results. A question many people miss usually points to a step that needs better text or a clearer shot.

The supervisor still watches the person do the task and signs them off on the floor.

Keeping it current

Give each video SOP an owner. When the equipment, recipe or layout changes, the owner updates it.

Replace only the step that changed. Re-filming one clip is faster than a full re-shoot.

Publish the new version and make sure people who learned the old one see the change.

Review each video SOP on a set schedule, for example every six months, even if nothing seems to have changed.

A new task added to the library should go through the same review as the first one. Speed of updating is only useful if the update is right.

## Video SOP mistakes to avoid

Most video SOPs fail because they are too long, too general or out of date. These are the mistakes to watch for.

Filming a whole shift in one video. Nobody replays minute 14 of a 20 minute clip. One task per video, cut into steps.

Filming the manager instead of the expert. The person who does the job daily knows the small tricks that matter.

Keeping numbers only in the speech. If the temperature is said once over the noise of a hood fan, it is lost. Put it in the text.

Filming the ideal, not the real. Use the station, tools and layout people actually have.

Showing a shortcut by accident. Watch for missing gloves, skipped checks or a guard left open. Re-film the step.

No owner. Without one person responsible, the video drifts out of date and people stop trusting it.

Treating a watched video as a trained person. A quiz shows understanding. Doing the job correctly under supervision is still the sign-off.

## Questions

**How long should a video SOP be?**
As long as one task takes, cut into short steps. Most steps should be short enough to replay at the station without scrolling, often under a minute. If the whole video runs long, check whether it is really two or three tasks and split it. The length of the task matters less than whether each step shows one action with one result.

**Do I need professional equipment to make a video SOP?**
No. A recent phone, steady hands or a small stand, and decent light are enough. Sound matters more than picture quality, so film in a quieter moment and put key facts in the step text. A professional shoot often looks better but is slower to update, which matters more over time.

**Should a video SOP have narration?**
Yes, if the worker can explain as they go in plain words. Their voice adds the why behind each step. Do not rely on narration alone: workplaces are loud and people may watch with the sound off, so every number, limit and warning should also appear as text on the step.

**Can a video SOP replace hands-on training?**
No. It replaces the repeated showing and explaining, so a trainer does not demonstrate the same task many times. The person still practices the task, and a supervisor still watches them do it and signs them off. A quiz shows who understood the steps, not who can do the job.

**How often should video SOPs be updated?**
Whenever the equipment, recipe, layout or rule changes, and on a fixed review schedule even if nothing seems to have changed. Give each video SOP an owner who is responsible for both. Update only the step that changed and make sure people who learned the old version see the new one.

**Is a video SOP enough for a food safety or safety audit?**
It depends on the rules that apply to you, so check them with your local authority or advisor. A clear, approved procedure with a record of who was trained can support an audit. Many auditors still expect written procedures with exact values, which is why each step should carry its key facts as text.

# SOP template and how to write an SOP (with example)
URL: https://www.flexlore.com/guides/sop-template/
Language: en

An SOP (standard operating procedure) is an approved, step-by-step description of how one recurring task is done, so anyone trained on it gets the same result. To write one, watch the best person do the task, split it into single-action steps written as commands, add photos or video, test it with a new hire, approve it and schedule reviews.

## What is an SOP?

An SOP (standard operating procedure) is a written, approved description of how one recurring task is done in your business, step by step, so anyone trained on it gets the same result. It answers four questions: what the task is, who does it, what they need, and exactly what they do.
An SOP is not a policy. A policy says what must be true ("the fryer station is cleaned every night"). An SOP says how to make it true ("turn off the fryer, wait for the oil to cool, drain it into the caddy"). Teams that mix the two end up with documents nobody can follow on a busy shift.
Good SOPs share three traits. They cover one task with a clear start and end. They are written in the order the work happens, not the order someone remembered it. And they have an owner who keeps them current. If a new hire can open the SOP at 7am on their second day and close the station correctly without asking anyone, it works.

## What sections does an SOP need?

A usable SOP needs a short header and nine sections: purpose, scope, roles, materials and tools, safety notes, steps, quality check, records and revision history. Keep each section short. Most of the reader's attention should land on the steps.
Section | What goes in it | Common mistake | 
Header | Title, SOP number, area, version, owner, approver, effective date, next review date | No owner, so nobody updates it | 
Purpose | One or two sentences on why the task matters | A paragraph of company values | 
Scope | Where and when it applies, and what it does not cover | Leaving out exceptions (late close, holiday menu) | 
Roles | Who does the task, who checks it, who to call when something is off | Names instead of roles, so it breaks when people leave | 
Materials and tools | Everything needed before step 1 | Discovering a missing tool at step 6 | 
Safety notes | Hazards, protective equipment, what never to do | Burying warnings inside steps | 
Steps | Numbered actions in the order the work happens | Several actions packed into one step | 
Quality check | What "done right" looks like, and how to check it | No standard, so "done" means "stopped" | 
Records | What gets logged, where, and by whom | Logs that exist but nobody reads | 
Revision history | Version, date, what changed, who approved | Silent edits nobody is told about | 
If the task is short and low risk, you can merge purpose and scope into one line. Do not drop safety notes or the quality check, even on simple tasks. Those two sections are what make an SOP more than a to-do list.

## How to write an SOP in 7 steps

Write an SOP by watching the best person do the task, breaking it into steps, writing each step as a short command, adding photos or video, testing it with a new hire, getting it approved, and putting a review date on it. Here is each step in practice.
1. Observe the person who does it best
Do not write from memory or from an old binder. Stand next to your strongest cook, operator or housekeeper and watch them do the job from start to finish. Ask why they do things in that order. The small habits they no longer notice (wiping the gasket, checking the drain valve twice) are usually what separates a good result from a bad one.
2. Break the task into steps
List every action in order. Then group them so each step is one action with one visible result. If a step needs the word "and" twice, split it. Mark the steps where mistakes are expensive or dangerous; those get a key point or a warning.
3. Write each step in the imperative
Start each step with a verb: turn, check, drain, record. Use the words people use on the floor, not the words in the manual. Add the reason when the reason changes behavior ("Wait until the oil is below the temperature on the safety label, because hot oil splashes when drained").
4. Add photos or video where words fall short
Some steps are hard to describe: how full is "full", what a clean filter looks like, how a part clicks into place. Show them. A short clip of the actual station often replaces a paragraph of text. A video SOP takes this further and makes the video the main format.
5. Test it with a new hire
Give the draft to someone who has never done the task and watch them follow it without help. Every time they hesitate or ask a question, the SOP has a gap. Fix it and test again. This step is the one most teams skip, and it is the one that matters most.
6. Get it approved
The person responsible for the area signs off on the final version. Approval makes the SOP the standard, not one person's opinion. Record the approver and the date in the header.
7. Set a review date
Put a review date on every SOP when it is published. Review sooner when equipment, menu, product or layout changes. An SOP that describes last year's machine trains people to make mistakes.

## Good vs bad SOP step wording

A good step tells one person to do one thing they can see and check. A bad step is vague, passive or packs several actions together. Compare these rewrites.
Bad step | Good step | Why it is better | 
The fryer should be cleaned properly. | Scrub the inside walls of the fry pot with the long-handled brush. | Starts with a verb, names the tool, says where | 
Make sure oil is cool. | Check that the oil is below the temperature on the fryer's safety label before you open the drain valve. | Gives a check, not a feeling | 
Drain oil, filter it, refill and turn on. | Split into four steps: drain, filter, refill, switch on. | One action per step, easier to follow and to check | 
Be careful with chemicals. | Wear gloves and goggles when you pour the degreaser. | Names the protection and the moment it is needed | 
Log it. | Write the time and your initials on the closing log on the station clipboard. | Says what, where and who | 
Read each step aloud. If you would not say it that way to a new hire standing at the station, rewrite it.

## Which SOP format should you use?

Use a simple numbered-step format for most frontline tasks, a checklist for routines people already know, a flowchart for tasks with decisions, and video for tasks that depend on hands and timing. Many teams combine two.
Numbered steps: the default. Works for opening and closing routines, cleaning, prep and setup.
Checklist: a short version for experienced staff who need a reminder, not training. Keep the full SOP behind it.
Flowchart: for tasks with branches, such as "if the reading is out of range, do this".
Video: for tasks where the hands matter more than the words, like folding, plating, threading a film or setting a blade.
For a single machine task done at one station, a work instruction is often a better fit than a full SOP. It is narrower and more detailed at each step.

## How do you keep SOPs up to date?

Keep SOPs current by giving each one an owner, a review date and a simple change process, and by telling people when a procedure changes. Out-of-date SOPs are worse than none, because they teach the old way with authority.
One owner per SOP. A role, not a name: "kitchen manager", "line 2 lead".
Review on a schedule. Set the interval by risk: high-risk tasks more often, low-risk ones less.
Review on change. New equipment, new supplier, new menu item, new layout, or an incident all trigger a review.
Collect feedback from the floor. The people doing the task notice gaps first. Make it easy for them to flag a step.
Retrain after changes. Updating the document is half the job. The team that learned the old version needs to see what changed, and you need to know who has.
Remove old copies. One current version, in one place. Printed copies at stations should carry the version number so anyone can spot an outdated one.
Track who has been trained on which version. A training matrix is the usual way to see that by person and task.

## Should an SOP be written or filmed?

Film the tasks that are hard to describe and keep a short written version for reference and audits. Most frontline jobs are physical, and people learn them faster by watching than by reading a page.
A filmed SOP works best when it is split into short steps that match the written ones, so a new hire can replay just the step they are stuck on. Film the best person at the real station, in normal light, with the real tools. Keep the camera on the hands. Add a line of text to each step with the action and any key point.
Written text still matters. It is searchable, quick to scan and easy to approve. The strongest setup is both: a video for each step, the written instruction beside it, and a short quiz at the end to check the steps were understood. Signing someone off as able to do the task on the floor stays with their supervisor.

## SOP template: Closing the fryer station

SOP TEMPLATE (example: Closing the fryer station)

Field	Example entry
SOP title	Closing the fryer station
SOP number	SOP-KIT-014
Area	Kitchen, fry station
Version	3
Owner	Kitchen manager
Approved by	Operations manager
Effective date	[date]
Next review	[date]
Time needed	About 25 minutes

PURPOSE
Leave the fryers clean, safe and ready for the opening shift, with oil that is filtered or changed on schedule.

SCOPE
Applies to both fryers at the end of every service. Does not cover deep cleaning (boil-out), which has its own SOP.

ROLES
Closing cook does the task. Shift lead checks it and signs the closing log. Call the kitchen manager if the oil looks dark or foamy before its scheduled change, or if a fryer shows a fault.

MATERIALS AND TOOLS
Oil caddy, filter paper, long-handled fryer brush, scraper, lint-free cloths, degreaser, heat-resistant gloves, goggles, apron, fryer covers, closing log.

SAFETY NOTES
Never drain hot oil. Never add water to a fryer with oil in it. Wear heat-resistant gloves, goggles and apron for steps 3 to 9. Keep the floor around the station dry; put a wet-floor sign out if anything spills.

STEPS
1. Switch both fryers off at the control panel and lift the baskets out.
2. Let the oil cool until it is below the temperature on the fryer's safety label. Check the reading, do not guess.
3. Put on heat-resistant gloves, goggles and apron.
4. Remove the baskets and wash them at the pot sink.
5. Skim crumbs from the surface of the oil with the skimmer.
6. Place the oil caddy under the drain valve and check it is locked in position.
7. Open the drain valve slowly and drain the oil into the caddy through fresh filter paper.
8. Scrub the inside walls and heating elements with the long-handled brush. Scrape off any buildup at the bottom.
9. Close the drain valve, then return the filtered oil to the fryer, or fill with fresh oil if today is a change day on the log.
10. Wipe the outside, the control panel and the hood edge with degreaser and a clean cloth.
11. Put the clean, dry baskets back and cover both fryers.
12. Record the time, oil status (filtered or changed) and your initials on the closing log.

QUALITY CHECK
Drain valve closed, oil at the fill line, no crumbs in the oil, no grease on the outside or panel, covers on, floor dry. The shift lead checks and initials the log.

RECORDS
Closing log on the station clipboard. The kitchen manager reviews it weekly and keeps it for the period your local rules require.

REVISION HISTORY
Version	Date	Change	Approved by
1	[date]	First version	Operations manager
2	[date]	Added filter paper step after new caddy	Operations manager
3	[date]	Split draining and scrubbing into separate steps after new-hire test	Operations manager


## Questions

**How long should an SOP be?**
As long as the task needs and no longer. Most frontline SOPs fit on one or two pages with 8 to 15 steps. If yours runs much longer, it probably covers more than one task. Split it at natural break points, such as opening versus closing, or setup versus cleaning, and link the parts together.

**What is the difference between an SOP and a work instruction?**
An SOP describes a whole process: who is involved, when it happens, what it covers and the main steps. A work instruction zooms in on one task at one station, with more detail per step, such as key points, tool settings and the reason behind each action. Many teams keep both and link them.

**Who should write an SOP?**
The person who does the task best should shape the content, and the person responsible for the area should own and approve it. A trainer or manager often does the writing, but should do it while watching the real work, not from memory. A new hire then tests the draft before it is published.

**How often should SOPs be reviewed?**
Set a review date on every SOP and base the interval on risk: tasks involving safety, food handling or expensive equipment need more frequent reviews than low-risk routines. Review immediately when equipment, product, layout or local rules change, or after an incident or a near miss. Check your local regulations for any required interval.

**Does a written SOP make my business compliant?**
No document makes a business compliant by itself. A clear, approved, current SOP with training records can support an audit or inspection, because it shows what the standard is and who was trained on it. Which procedures you must document and keep depends on your industry and local rules, so check those directly.

**Can an SOP be a video instead of a document?**
Yes, and for physical tasks video often teaches faster than text. The best setup pairs short video steps with a written line for each, so the SOP is easy to watch, scan and approve. Keep a version number and approval record for the video just as you would for a document.

# Work instruction template: how to write standard work instructions
URL: https://www.flexlore.com/guides/work-instruction-template/
Language: en

A work instruction is a step-by-step guide for one task at one station, such as a blade change or machine setup. Each step gives an action, a key point that decides quality or safety, and the reason. An SOP describes the wider process; the work instruction shows the operator exactly how to do one part of it.

## What is a work instruction?

A work instruction is a step-by-step guide for one task at one station, written so an operator can do it correctly the first time and the same way every time. It sits below an SOP: the SOP describes the process, the work instruction shows exactly how to do one part of it.
Think of a changeover on packaging line 2 at the start of the night shift. The SOP says line changeovers follow lockout, are done by a trained operator, and are checked before restart. The work instruction says which guard to open, which bolts to loosen in which order, what the blade gap should look like and why you never skip the test cut.
In many plants this format is called standard work instruction or job instruction. The name matters less than the content: one task, steps in order, the key points that make the result good or safe, and the reason behind each key point.

## SOP vs work instruction vs checklist: what is the difference?

An SOP covers a whole process and who is responsible for it, a work instruction details one task at one station, and a checklist reminds a trained person what to confirm. They work best as a set, each linked to the next.
 | SOP | Work instruction | Checklist | 
Answers | What happens, who does it, when | Exactly how to do this task | Did I do everything | 
Scope | A process, often across roles | One task, one station or machine | One routine or inspection | 
Detail per step | Medium | High: key points, settings, reasons | Low: one line per item | 
Main reader | Managers, leads, auditors, trainees | Operator at the station | Trained operator | 
Used for training | Context and overview | Yes, the main training tool | No, a reminder after training | 
Example | Line changeover procedure | Changing the cutting blade on line 2 | Pre-start check on line 2 | 
A simple rule: if a new operator could follow the document alone at the machine, it is a work instruction. If they would still need someone to show them, it is an SOP or a checklist. For the process-level document, see our SOP template.

## What does a good work instruction include?

A good work instruction covers one task at one station, lists everything needed before the first step, and gives each step an action, a key point and the reason for that key point. Quality and safety steps are marked so nobody misses them.
One task, one station. "Changing the cutting blade on line 2", not "Line 2 maintenance". If the task changes stations, start a new instruction.
A header. Part or product, station, tools, protective equipment, expected time, revision number, owner and approver.
Steps in order. Each one an action the operator can see and check.
Key points. The detail that decides whether the step is done right: the bolt order, the gap, the click, the torque setting on your tool.
Reasons. Why the key point matters. People who know the reason remember the step and handle the unusual case better.
Marks for quality and safety. Label the steps where a mistake causes scrap, a defect or an injury, for example with "Safety" or "Quality" at the start of the key point.
A finish check. What the operator confirms before handing the machine back: a test cut, a first-piece check, a sign-off.

## How to write work instructions for the shop floor

Write each step as a verb first, one action per step, and put the key point and its reason next to it. Use the words operators use at the machine, and test the draft with someone who has never done the task.
Start each step with a verb
"Loosen the four blade bolts" beats "The blade bolts should be loosened". Verb first tells the operator what to do before they finish reading.
One action per step
If a step needs two verbs, it is usually two steps. This makes the instruction longer on paper and faster on the floor, because nobody loses their place.
Show the key point and the why
Split the step into three parts: the action (what), the key point (how to do it well or safely) and the reason (why). Operators who understand why the bolts are tightened in a cross pattern stop skipping it when the line is behind.
Watch the best operator first
Write from what the best person actually does, not from the machine manual. Ask them what they check without thinking about it. Those habits often become key points. This is the same idea behind master-to-apprentice skills transfer: capture the expert's method before it walks out the door.
Test it at the machine
Give the draft to an operator who has not done the task, and watch. Every pause or question is a missing key point. Fix it before you approve it.

## Visual and video work instructions

Use photos or video for any step where position, movement or feel matters more than words. A short clip of the real machine often shows a key point faster than a sentence can describe it.
Photos work for positions and end states: where the guard latch is, what a correct blade gap looks like, how the label should sit. Video works for movement and timing: how to feed film through the rollers, how hard to push a part until it seats, the order of hand movements in a changeover.
Keep each clip to one step and match it to the written step, so an operator can replay only the part they need. Film at the actual station, with the real tools and normal lighting, and keep the camera on the hands. A video SOP uses the same approach for full procedures.

## Work instructions for changeovers and machine setups

Changeovers and setups are where work instructions pay off most, because they happen often enough to matter and rarely enough that people forget the details. Write one instruction per changeover type and keep the steps in the order the work is done at the machine.
Split preparation from machine-stopped work. List what can be done while the line is still running (fetching tools, staging the new blade or die, reading the job sheet) separately from what needs the machine stopped.
Start with your lockout steps. Refer to your site's lockout procedure by name and mark the step as safety. Do not paraphrase it in a way that could drift from the original.
Record settings, not memories. Put the settings for each product in a table in the instruction or the job sheet, so the next shift does not rely on whoever set it last.
End with a first-piece check. Define what a good first part looks like and who approves it before the line goes back to full speed.
Changeovers are also a good place to cross-train: an operator who has done the same changeover from a clear instruction a few times can cover a shift when the usual person is out.

## How to manage versions at the station

Keep one current version of each work instruction, show the revision number where operators can see it, and retrain people when it changes. An old copy taped to the machine is the most common reason operators follow the wrong steps.
Revision number on every page or screen. Operators and leads should be able to check it at a glance.
One owner. Usually the area lead or process engineer. They approve every change.
Change triggers. New tooling, a new product, a quality issue, a near miss or operator feedback all prompt a review.
Pull old copies. When a new version is approved, remove printed copies of the old one from the station the same day.
Track who learned which version. After a change, you need to know which operators have seen the new steps before they run the machine again.

## Doing this with Flexlore

With Flexlore you film the best operator doing the task on a phone, mark the steps in the phone video editor, and AI drafts the written step instructions and a short quiz. Your team reviews and approves the draft before anyone sees it. Operators watch the steps on their own phone, replay the one they need, and take the quiz; you see who has watched and passed, by person, team and location. Roles and workspaces keep each site's instructions separate. Signing an operator off on the machine stays with their supervisor. QR codes on the machine that open the right instruction, and automatic translation, are coming soon. See how it fits manufacturing teams.

## Work instruction template: Changing the cutting blade on packaging line 2

WORK INSTRUCTION TEMPLATE (example: Changing the cutting blade on packaging line 2)

Field	Example entry
Work instruction	Changing the cutting blade on packaging line 2
Document number	WI-PK2-005
Part / product	Flow-wrap knife blade, all film types
Station	Packaging line 2, cutting unit
Tools	10 mm hex key, torque wrench, feeler gauge, guard key, lint-free cloth, blade box
PPE	Cut-resistant gloves, safety glasses, safety shoes
Time	About 15 minutes
Revision	Rev 4, [date]
Owner / approved by	Line 2 lead / Production manager

Step	Action	Key point	Why
1	Stop the line at the control panel and wait until the knife drum stops turning.	Safety: never open the guard while the drum is moving.	The drum keeps turning for several seconds after stop.
2	Apply your lock and tag at the main disconnect, following the site lockout procedure.	Safety: use your own lock. Try the start button to confirm zero energy.	Someone else could restart the line while your hands are inside.
3	Put on cut-resistant gloves and safety glasses.	Gloves stay on until the old blade is in the blade box.	Blade edges cut through normal work gloves.
4	Open the knife guard with the guard key.	Lift the guard until the latch clicks open.	A half-open guard can drop onto your hands.
5	Loosen the four blade bolts with the 10 mm hex key, outside bolts first.	Do not remove the inside bolts yet.	The inside bolts hold the blade while you work.
6	Remove the inside bolts and lift the old blade out by the spine.	Hold the blade by the spine, never the edge.	The edge is still sharp even when it no longer cuts film cleanly.
7	Put the old blade straight into the blade box.	Never leave a blade on the machine frame.	A loose blade can fall into the drum or injure the next person.
8	Wipe the blade seat with a lint-free cloth.	Check there is no film or adhesive left on the seat.	Dirt under the blade changes the cutting gap.
9	Fit the new blade with the bevel facing the drum.	Quality: check the bevel direction against the sticker on the guard.	A reversed blade tears film instead of cutting it.
10	Fit all four bolts by hand, then tighten them in a cross pattern with the torque wrench at the setting on the job sheet.	Quality: cross pattern, two passes.	Uneven tightening bends the blade and gives a ragged cut.
11	Check the blade gap with the feeler gauge at both ends.	Quality: the gauge slides with light drag at both ends.	An uneven gap cuts one side and tears the other.
12	Close the guard, remove your lock and tag, and restart the line at crawl speed.	Safety: check everyone is clear before removing the lock.	The line restarts with whoever is closest to it.
13	Run 5 test cuts and check the edges.	Quality: clean, straight edges with no strings or tears.	Confirms the blade and gap before full-speed production.
14	Record the blade change, time and your initials on the line 2 log, and tell the shift lead.	Write the blade lot number from the box.	Lets quality trace a cutting problem back to a blade.

FINISH CHECK
Guard closed and latched, lock removed, 5 clean test cuts, log filled in, shift lead informed. If any test cut tears, stop the line and repeat steps 1, 2 and 11.


## Questions

**What is the difference between an SOP and a work instruction?**
An SOP describes a process: what happens, who is responsible, when and in what order. A work instruction details one task inside that process at one station, with key points, settings and reasons for each step. An SOP might say changeovers follow lockout and a first-piece check; the work instruction shows how to change the blade on line 2.

**What is a key point in a work instruction?**
A key point is the detail that decides whether a step is done well or safely: the bolt order, the gap, the click when a part seats, the side a bevel faces. Most steps have one at most. Writing them down, with the reason, is what turns an expert's habits into something a new operator can repeat.

**How detailed should a work instruction be?**
Detailed enough that a trained but new operator can do the task alone at the machine. Every action gets a step, every step that affects quality or safety gets a key point, and the key point gets a reason. If an operator still needs someone beside them to finish the task, something is missing.

**Should work instructions include photos or video?**
Yes, for any step where position, movement or feel matters. Photos are good for end states such as a correct gap or a seated part. Short video clips are better for movement, like threading film or the order of hand movements. Match each image or clip to one written step so operators can find it quickly.

**Who approves a work instruction?**
The person responsible for the area, usually the line lead, process engineer or production manager, approves each version. The best operator should review it for accuracy, and a new operator should test it at the machine first. Record the approver and revision number in the header so anyone can check they have the current version.

**Where should work instructions be kept?**
Where the operator needs them: at the station, on a screen or on their phone, always as the current version. Keep the master copy in one controlled place, show the revision number on every copy, and remove old printed copies when a new version is approved. Out-of-date copies at the machine cause more mistakes than missing ones.

# Training matrix template: build a skills matrix your shifts can use
URL: https://www.flexlore.com/guides/training-matrix-template/
Language: en

A training matrix (also called a skills or competency matrix) is a grid with people in rows and jobs in columns. Each cell holds a skill level, usually 0 to 4, so a manager can see who can run each station, where a shift has no cover, and who is ready to train others.

## What is a training matrix?

A training matrix is a table that shows who can do which job, and how well. People go down the side, jobs or skills go across the top, and each cell holds a level from a fixed scale.
You will see it called a skills matrix, a competency matrix or a cross training matrix. The names overlap. In practice, a training matrix often tracks whether training happened, while a skills or competency matrix tracks whether the person can actually do the work. The useful version does both: it records the level and the proof behind it.
On a restaurant line the columns are stations: grill, fryer, prep, expo, dish, opening and closing. On a production line they are machines and tasks: start-up, changeover, quality check, packing. In a hotel they are room turn, public areas, check-in and night audit. The structure is the same everywhere.

## What is a skills matrix used for?

A skills matrix answers the questions a manager asks before every rota: can this shift run if one person calls in sick, and who should learn what next.
Coverage per shift. Count how many independent people each station has on each shift. If the PM shift has one person who can run expo, you know where the risk sits before Friday night shows it to you.
Cross-training. The matrix shows who is one level away from covering a second station. That is your cheapest training: a line cook at level 2 on fryer needs a few supervised shifts, not a full course.
Single points of failure. Any column with only one person at level 3 or above is a job that stops when that person is on leave or moves on.
Who can train whom. Level 4 marks the people a new hire should shadow. Without it, new staff learn from whoever is free, and the job drifts a little with every handover.
Scheduling and hiring. When a gap will not close with cross-training, the matrix tells you which skill to hire for.
If shift resilience is the main reason you are building one, the post on cross-training for shift resilience covers how to choose which people to cross-train first.

## How to build a training matrix in 7 steps

Start with one location and one team, keep the columns to the jobs that actually stop the operation, and fill it in with the shift leads, not from the office.
List the jobs, not the job titles. Write down the tasks someone must be able to do for a shift to run: stations, machines, opening, closing, cash, deliveries. Ten to fifteen columns is a workable size for one team.
Make sure each job has a written standard. A level only means something if everyone agrees what "to standard" looks like. If a job has no SOP yet, note it and use a simple SOP template to write one.
List the people and their shifts. Add role and usual shift to each row. Shift is what lets you read coverage later.
Agree the level scale. Use five levels, 0 to 4, with the definitions below. Print them at the top of the sheet so every rater uses the same words.
Rate with the person who watches the work. The shift lead or supervisor rates each cell. Where you are unsure, rate lower and plan an observation.
Add coverage rows. Under each column, count the people at level 3 or 4 per shift and set a target, for example two per shift for every station.
Turn gaps into a training plan. For each column below target, pick one person at level 1 or 2, name a trainer at level 4 and set a date to check again.
A spreadsheet is enough to start. Use one tab per location, freeze the first three columns, and add color by level so gaps stand out when you scroll.

## Which skill level scale should you use?

Use a five-step scale from 0 (not trained) to 4 (can train others), and tie each level to a piece of evidence. Levels without evidence turn into opinions.
Level | Definition | How it is earned | 
0 Not trained | Has not been shown the job. | Starting point for every new job. | 
1 In training | Has seen the job and is learning it next to a trainer. | Watched the job and did it with a trainer beside them. | 
2 Can do with support | Does the job on a live shift; someone trained checks it. | Passed a short quiz on the steps and worked supervised shifts. | 
3 Independent | Does the job alone, to standard, at normal pace. | Supervisor watched them do it on a real shift and signed off. | 
4 Can train others | Independent and able to teach and check the job. | Chosen by the manager; has trained someone to level 3. | 
Keep the gap between 2 and 3 strict. Level 3 means you would leave that person alone on the station during a rush. If the honest answer is "not yet", it is a 2.
Some teams add a date to each cell, or a letter for "due for refresh". That is useful for jobs that change often or are done rarely, like deep cleaning a fryer or a quarterly machine check.

## How to read a training matrix: gaps and coverage per shift

Read the matrix by column first, then by row. Columns show where the operation is fragile; rows show who to develop next.
Read the columns
Count level 3 and 4 per shift. Below target is a coverage gap.
A column with one name at 3 or above is a single point of failure.
A column with no level 4 has nobody to train the next person. Fix this before the next hire arrives.
Read the rows
Level 2 cells are your quickest wins: a few supervised shifts and a sign-off.
A row full of 3s and 4s is a strong candidate for trainer or shift lead.
A row that has not moved in months may point to a scheduling issue (always on the same station) rather than a training one.
In the example template below, the kitchen looks well staffed, but expo has only one independent person per shift, prep on the PM shift depends on one cook, and nobody can train the cold station. Those three gaps are the training plan for the next month.

## How do you keep a skills matrix current?

Link every level to proof that is recorded when it happens: watched the job, passed the quiz, signed off by the supervisor. A matrix updated once a year from memory is out of date within weeks.
Watched the job. The person has seen the current version of the job, step by step. This supports level 1.
Passed the quiz. A short quiz on the steps shows they understood the standard: temperatures, order of steps, what not to skip. This supports level 2. A quiz drafted from the job itself keeps the questions tied to how the work is really done.
Signed off on the floor. A supervisor watches them do the job on a real shift and confirms it. Only this supports level 3. A quiz shows understanding; it does not replace watching someone work.
Update the matrix at a fixed moment, for example at the weekly rota meeting. When a job changes (a new recipe, a new machine setting), drop affected people back to level 2 until they have seen the new version and been checked again.

## How to run a training matrix across several locations

Use the same columns and the same level scale in every location, and keep one matrix per location. Then you can compare sites line by line.
When columns differ between sites, comparisons stop working: one store calls it "fry station", another splits it into "fries" and "chicken". Agree the job list centrally, and let a location add a column only for equipment it alone has.
For a franchise or multi-site group, roll the coverage rows up into one summary: for each location, which stations are below target on which shift. That summary is what an area manager needs before a visit. People who work at more than one site should appear in each matrix where they cover shifts, with the same levels.
Access matters too. Store managers should edit their own matrix, and the area manager should see all of them. Tools with roles and workspaces by location make this easier than a shared spreadsheet that everyone can overwrite.

## Common training matrix mistakes

Too many columns. Forty skills per person means nobody updates it. Track the jobs that stop a shift; keep the rest in the job description.
Levels without definitions. "3" means something different to every shift lead unless the scale is written down with examples.
Rating from the office. The person who sees the work every day should rate it.
No evidence behind a level. When someone asks "why is she a 3 on grill", the answer should be a date and a supervisor name.
Never lowering a level. When the job changes or someone has not done it in months, the honest level is lower.
Treating it as paperwork. The matrix should change the rota and the training plan. If it never does, it is not being read.

## Doing this with Flexlore

Flexlore covers the evidence side of a training matrix. A team member films a job on a phone at the station, marks the steps in the phone editor, and AI drafts the written steps and a short quiz. Your team reviews and approves every draft before it goes out.
Once a job is assigned, you see who has watched it and who passed its quiz, by person, team and location. That covers levels 1 and 2. Level 3 stays with your supervisor, who signs people off on the floor. Roles and workspaces keep each location to its own jobs. Apps run on iOS and Android, in 8 languages. A web panel for managers and notifications are coming soon. Plans are by number of users; see pricing.

## Training matrix template (kitchen example)

LEVEL LEGEND
Level	Name	What it means on the floor	Evidence to record
0	Not trained	Has not been shown the job. Should not work the station.	None
1	In training	Has watched the job and is learning it with a trainer next to them.	Watched the job video or demo
2	Can do with support	Does the job on a real shift, but a trained person checks the work and steps in when needed.	Passed the short quiz on the steps
3	Independent	Does the job alone, to standard, at normal pace, on a busy shift.	Signed off by a supervisor after watching them work
4	Can train others	Independent, and can teach and check the job for someone else.	Picked by the manager as a trainer for this job

EXAMPLE: KITCHEN SKILLS MATRIX, ONE LOCATION
Person	Role	Shift	Grill	Fryer	Prep	Cold station	Expo / pass	Dish	Opening	Closing
Cook A	Lead cook	AM	4	4	3	3	4	3	4	2
Cook B	Line cook	AM	3	3	2	1	2	3	3	0
Cook E	Prep cook	AM	0	1	4	3	0	3	3	0
Cook C	Line cook	PM	3	2	3	3	1	3	0	3
Cook D	Line cook	PM	1	3	2	2	0	3	0	2
Shift lead H	Shift lead	PM	3	3	2	3	3	3	2	4
Dishwasher F	Dishwasher	PM	0	0	1	0	0	4	0	3
New hire G	Line cook (week 2)	PM	0	1	1	0	0	2	0	0

COVERAGE ROWS (count the 3s and 4s per shift)
Coverage check			Grill	Fryer	Prep	Cold station	Expo / pass	Dish	Opening	Closing
Level 3+ on AM			2	2	2	2	1	3	3	n/a
Level 3+ on PM			2	2	1	2	1	4	n/a	3
Level 4 (trainers)			1	1	1	0	1	1	1	1
Target per shift			2	2	2	2	2	2	2	2

What this example shows: expo has only one independent person per shift, prep on PM depends on Cook C alone, and nobody can train the cold station yet. Those are the next three training priorities.

## Questions

**What is the difference between a training matrix and a skills matrix?**
The terms are used for the same grid. A training matrix often records whether training was delivered, while a skills or competency matrix records whether the person can do the job to standard. The most useful version records both: the level, and the evidence behind it, such as a passed quiz or a supervisor sign-off.

**How many skill levels should a competency matrix have?**
Four or five levels work for most frontline teams. A 0 to 4 scale (not trained, in training, can do with support, independent, can train others) is easy to explain on the floor. Fewer levels hide progress, and more levels make raters disagree about the difference between neighboring scores.

**How often should a skills matrix be updated?**
Update it whenever a level changes, and review it at a fixed moment such as the weekly rota meeting. When a job changes, for example a new recipe or machine setting, move the people affected back a level until they have seen the new version and been checked again.

**Can I make a training matrix in Excel or Google Sheets?**
Yes. Put people and shifts in the first columns, jobs across the top, and a number from 0 to 4 in each cell. Add color by level, freeze the first columns, and add coverage rows that count level 3 and 4 per shift. Use one tab per location with the same columns.

**Who should fill in the training matrix?**
The supervisor or shift lead who sees the work every day should rate each cell, ideally after watching the person do the job. HR or the manager can own the file and the level definitions, but ratings made from the office tend to be too generous and go out of date fast.

**Does passing a quiz mean someone is competent?**
No. A quiz shows a person understood the steps and the standard. Competence on the job is confirmed when a supervisor watches them do it on a real shift and signs them off. In the matrix, a passed quiz supports level 2, and a sign-off supports level 3.

# Restaurant onboarding checklist: the first 30 days for new hires
URL: https://www.flexlore.com/guides/restaurant-onboarding-checklist/
Language: en

A restaurant onboarding checklist lists what a new hire must see, do and prove before working a station alone. Split it into before day one, day one, the first week and days 8 to 30, give every item an owner, and close each station with a short quiz and a supervisor sign-off on the floor.

## What should a restaurant onboarding checklist include?

A restaurant onboarding checklist should cover four stages (before day one, day one, the first week and days 8 to 30), name an owner for every item, and end each station with a check: a short quiz on the steps and a supervisor sign-off on the floor.
Most restaurant onboarding fails in a predictable way. The new hire gets a quick tour, gets put on a station next to whoever is free, and learns that person's version of the job. Three weeks later nobody is sure what they were shown. A checklist fixes that by making the first month the same for every new hire, whatever shift they start on.
Good checklists share a few traits:
Owners, not just tasks. "Allergen procedure" with no name next to it does not happen on a Saturday.
Station by station. Front of house, kitchen and dish learn different jobs at different speeds.
A check at the end of each stage. Watching is not the same as understanding, and understanding is not the same as doing it at 8pm with twelve tickets on the rail.
For why programs without these break down, see why new hire onboarding programs fail.

## Before day one: paperwork, schedule and a buddy

Everything that can be done before the first shift should be done before it, so day one is spent on the floor and not in the office.
Send the start date, the first shift time, where to enter and who to ask for. A new hire waiting at the front door during service is a bad first hour.
Finish hiring paperwork and any eligibility checks your location requires.
Check which food handler training, health certificates or permits your local rules require for this role, and whether they must be done before the first shift. Requirements differ by country, state and city, so follow your local authority rather than a generic list.
Get uniform, apron and name badge ready. Tell them what footwear to bring.
Pick a buddy: someone who does the first station well and can explain it. Put both on the same shifts for the first week.

## Day one: what a new hire needs to see first

Day one is for safety, hygiene and one station, not the whole menu. Keep it to what they need to work safely next to others.
Welcome and the team. Introduce them to whoever is on shift, including the dish and FOH crew.
Tour. Staff entrance, lockers, toilets, fire exits, first aid kit, fire extinguishers, where chemicals are kept.
Handwashing. Where the sinks are, when to wash and how, to your house standard.
Food safety and allergens. The basics your local rules and your own standard require: holding temperatures, labeling, storage order and exactly how an allergen order is flagged and handled.
Safety on the floor. Knives, hot oil, wet floors, lifting, and who to tell when something goes wrong. New staff are more exposed in their first weeks; the post on the first-month safety gap covers why.
Shadow the first station. Part of a shift next to the buddy, watching and helping.
Check-in before they leave. Five minutes: what was confusing, what is next.

## First week: shadow, then do it with support

In week one the new hire learns one station properly: watch the job, do it beside the buddy, then answer a few questions on it.
A typical week for a new line cook: day two watching the fryer jobs (oil check, basket loads, holding times) and running baskets with the buddy calling the tickets. Day three and four, the same station on a busier shift. By day five they run the station with the buddy nearby, and take a short quiz on each job they have watched.
Also in week one:
One opening or closing routine, shadowed.
How tickets reach their station and how calls on the pass work.
The station's cleaning schedule and end-of-shift breakdown.
A day 7 check-in with the manager, and an update of their row in the training matrix.

## Days 8 to 30: station by station

From week two, each role follows its own track. The goal by day 30 is a supervisor sign-off on the first station and a clear plan for the second.
Front of house
Greeting, seating and table maintenance to your standard.
Taking an order, menu and allergen questions, passing allergen orders to the kitchen.
POS: modifiers, voids, split bills, payments.
Running food and talking to the pass.
Handling a complaint and when to call a manager.
Kitchen
Prep list and par levels.
Every recipe and plating on the station, to spec.
Temperature checks and logs.
Labeling, dating and stock rotation.
Equipment start-up, cleaning and shutdown.
Dish
Dish machine set-up, chemical and temperature checks.
Sorting, racking, pots and putting away.
Safe handling of cleaning chemicals and where the safety information is kept.
Waste, recycling and grease.
Dish is often the first job new kitchen staff learn, and the one most often trained by whoever is free. Treat it as a station with its own checklist.

## What should you film once and reuse?

Film the jobs that every new hire needs and that are done the same way every time. Your best person does it once, on a phone, at the station, and every later hire learns that exact version.
Handwashing and glove use to your standard.
Allergen order handling, from order to plate.
Opening and closing for each station.
Recipes and plating for each item, one short video per dish.
Fryer oil check and filtering, grill clean-down.
Dish machine set-up and chemical check.
POS basics for FOH.
Keep each video to one job and split it into steps, so a cook can replay the one step they are unsure about. A one-time welcome is quickly forgotten without something to come back to; see the forgetting curve. Do not film what changes weekly, such as specials; a short note at line-up works better.

## How do you check that a new hire understood?

Use two checks: a short quiz right after each job, and a supervisor sign-off on the floor before they work a station alone.
The quiz should ask about what goes wrong in real life: "Which ticket marker means an allergen order?", "What do you do if the oil is below the line?", "Which shelf does raw chicken go on?" Three to five questions per job is enough. A quiz shows who understood the steps; it does not show who can do them under pressure.
The sign-off does that. A supervisor watches the new hire run the station on a real shift and confirms it in writing, with a date. Until that happens, the person works the station with support. Record both checks in your training matrix so the next manager can see where each person stands.

## How to keep onboarding the same across locations

Use one checklist, one set of job videos and one level scale for every location, and compare completion by location each month.
The central team owns the checklist and the job content. A location can add items for its own equipment, not change the shared ones.
Every new hire, in every store, watches the same version of each job.
Area managers look at completion and sign-offs by location to see which store needs a visit.
For high-volume or seasonal hiring, running several starts at once, see onboarding at speed.

## Common restaurant onboarding mistakes

Starting on the busiest shift. A Friday night start teaches survival, not the standard.
No named buddy. Learning from whoever is free gives a different version of the job each shift.
Everything on day one. A full menu, the POS and three stations in one shift does not stick.
Allergens covered verbally. This procedure needs to be shown, written down and checked.
No sign-off. "He seems fine" is not a check. Use a dated supervisor sign-off.
No day 30 review. The first month is when people decide whether to stay.

## Doing this with Flexlore

Flexlore handles the "film once and reuse" part of this checklist. Your best cook films a job on a phone at the station, marks the steps in the phone editor, and AI drafts the written steps and a short quiz. Your team reviews and approves every draft.
You assign jobs by role and location, and new hires watch on their own phone and replay any step. You see who watched each job and passed its quiz, by person, team and location. The sign-off on the floor stays with the supervisor. The app runs on iOS and Android in 8 languages. Automatic translation, QR codes at the station and notifications are coming soon. See how it fits a kitchen on the restaurants page.

DAYS 8 TO 30: KITCHEN
Item	Owner	Done
Prep list and par levels for the station	Kitchen lead	
Recipes and plating for every item on the station	Kitchen lead	
Temperature checks and logs	Kitchen lead	
Labeling, dating and stock rotation	Kitchen lead	
Equipment start-up, cleaning and shutdown	Kitchen lead	
Work the station on a busy shift with support	Buddy	

DAYS 8 TO 30: DISH
Item	Owner	Done
Dish machine set-up, chemical and temperature checks	Kitchen lead	
Sorting, racking, pot washing and putting away	Buddy	
Chemical handling and where the safety information is kept	Manager	
Waste, recycling and grease handling	Buddy	

DAYS 8 TO 30: ALL ROLES
Item	Owner	Done
Supervisor sign-off on each station before working it alone	Supervisor	
Second station started if the first is signed off	Manager	
Day 30 review: training matrix levels, next station, feedback both ways	Manager	

## Questions

**How long should restaurant onboarding take?**
Plan for about 30 days until a new hire is signed off on their first station, with the first week focused on safety, hygiene and one station. Simple roles can move faster and complex stations slower. What matters is that each station ends with a supervisor sign-off, not a fixed number of days.

**What should a new restaurant employee do on the first day?**
Meet the team on shift, tour the building including exits and first aid, learn handwashing and the basic food safety and allergen rules your location requires, hear who to tell when something goes wrong, and shadow one station for part of the shift. End with a short check-in with the manager.

**Who should train new restaurant staff?**
A named buddy who does the station well and can explain it, working the same shifts for the first week. The manager owns the checklist and the check-ins, and a supervisor signs off each station. Learning from whoever happens to be free gives a slightly different version of the job every shift.

**Does this checklist cover food safety requirements?**
It lists where food safety belongs in onboarding, but requirements such as food handler training, certificates and health checks are set by local rules and differ by country, state and city. Check with your local authority what applies to each role and when it must be completed, and add those items to the checklist.

**How do you check that new hires understood their training?**
Use a short quiz right after each job to check they understood the steps, then have a supervisor watch them run the station on a real shift and sign them off with a date. The quiz shows understanding; only the sign-off shows they can do the job under real conditions.

**How do you keep onboarding consistent across restaurant locations?**
Use one shared checklist, one set of job videos and one skill level scale everywhere. Let locations add items for their own equipment but not change shared ones, and compare completion and sign-offs by location each month so you can see which store needs support.


---

# SOP software: how to choose one for frontline teams
URL: https://www.flexlore.com/guides/sop-software/
Language: en

SOP software is a tool for creating, approving, sharing and updating standard operating procedures, and checking who has learned them. For frontline teams, choose one that works fully on a phone, supports video steps, checks understanding with a short quiz, controls access by role and location, tracks readiness and keeps every change approved.

## What does SOP software do?

SOP software is where a team creates, approves, shares and updates its standard operating procedures, and checks who has learned them. It replaces binders, shared folders and group chats with one library that people open on the job.

For frontline teams, good SOP software covers five jobs:

Create: build a procedure from video, photos or text without design or editing skills.

Approve: route drafts to the right person and keep a record of what was approved and when.

Share: send each procedure to the roles and locations that need it, on the phones people already carry.

Check: show who opened a procedure and who understood it, usually through a short quiz.

Update: change a step, publish a new version and make sure people see the change.

Office-focused document tools often do the first three well. The last two, and doing all of it on a phone at a station, are where frontline needs differ.

## Do you need SOP software, or will documents do?

Documents are enough while one person can keep everything in their head. You need SOP software when you cannot answer &quot;which version is current&quot; and &quot;who has been trained on it&quot; without asking around.

Signs you have outgrown documents:

Two locations do the same task differently, and both point to a document.

New hires learn by shadowing, and the result depends on who they shadow.

Printed procedures at the station are older than the equipment.

Nobody can say who has seen the new allergen or safety change.

One experienced person is the only one who really knows a job.

If none of these apply, a solid SOP template and a clear folder structure may be all you need for now.

## What to look for in SOP software for frontline teams

Judge SOP software by how well it works for the person at the fryer or on line 2, not the person at a desk. These are the criteria that matter most.

Mobile first

Frontline staff do not sit at computers. Creating, watching and approving should work fully on iOS and Android phones, not as a reduced version of a desktop tool.

Video, not only text

Physical tasks are easier to learn by watching. Look for the ability to film on a phone, trim, and split a video into steps with text on each. See our video SOP guide for what good looks like.

A check for understanding

&quot;Viewed&quot; is not &quot;understood&quot;. A short quiz after each procedure shows who got the key points. It should not pretend to replace a supervisor signing someone off on the floor.

Language support

Many frontline teams work in several languages. Check which languages the app itself runs in, and separately whether procedure content can be translated, and who checks the translation.

Roles and permissions by location

A franchise head office, a store manager and a new cashier need different access. Look for workspaces or groups by location, and roles that control who creates, approves and only views.

Readiness tracking

You should see, by person, team and location, who has completed each procedure and passed its check. This is the view an area manager opens on Monday morning.

Version control and approvals

Every change should go through approval, with a record of who approved what. People should always see the current version, and you should know who learned an older one.

Shop floor realities

Ask about weak signal in basements and cold rooms, shared devices, gloves, noise, and staff without company email addresses. If offline access matters to you, ask exactly what works without a connection.

Pricing by users

Most tools price by the number of users. Check what counts as a user, whether seasonal staff change your plan, and what limits apply to storage, quizzes or AI features.

## SOP software scoring checklist

Score each tool from 1 (poor) to 5 (strong) on every line, during a demo or trial, using one of your real tasks. Multiply by the weight you choose. The weights below are an example for a multi-location frontline team; change them to fit you.

Criterion | What to check | Example weight | Score (1 to 5) | 

Mobile creation | Can a shift lead film and publish a procedure from a phone? | 3 |  | 

Video steps | Can you trim and split a video into steps with text on each? | 3 |  | 

Understanding check | Is there a quiz per procedure, and can you edit the questions? | 2 |  | 

Approval flow | Does every draft need approval before staff see it? | 3 |  | 

Version history | Can you see what changed and who learned the old version? | 2 |  | 

Roles by location | Can access be limited by role and site? | 3 |  | 

Readiness view | Can you see completion and quiz results by person, team and location? | 3 |  | 

Languages | Which app languages exist today; is content translation available or planned? | 2 |  | 

Floor conditions | Offline behavior, shared devices, sign-in without company email | 2 |  | 

Ease for staff | Can a new hire find and finish a procedure without help? | 3 |  | 

Pricing fit | Does the user-based plan match your headcount and seasonal peaks? | 2 |  | 

Data and privacy | Are privacy, security and sub-processor details published? | 2 |  | 

Mark anything a vendor calls &quot;planned&quot; or &quot;coming soon&quot; separately. Score what exists today and treat the roadmap as a bonus, not a reason to buy.

## SOP software for restaurants, manufacturing and hotels: what changes?

The criteria stay the same; the weights change with the work.

Restaurants and cafés: high turnover and many locations put weight on mobile access, short video steps and readiness by location. Recipes, opening and closing routines and allergen steps are the usual first content. See restaurants.

Manufacturing: changeovers, machine start-up and safety steps put weight on approvals, version history and close-up video. Work instructions often sit next to the machine. See manufacturing.

Hotels: housekeeping and front desk standards put weight on clear visual standards and language support.

Franchises: head office needs to launch a process once and compare completion across locations, so roles by location and a readiness view matter most.

## Questions to ask in an SOP software demo

Bring one real task and ask the vendor to build it with you. Then ask these questions.

Can you show me a shift lead creating this procedure on a phone, start to finish?

What does the AI do, and what has to be approved by a person before staff see it?

How does a new hire find the right procedure at the station?

What does a manager see for one location, and for all locations together?

What happens to people who learned the old version when I change a step?

Which languages does the app run in today, and which features are on the roadmap rather than available?

What works without a connection?

Who counts as a user for pricing, and what happens in a seasonal peak?

Where is our data processed, and where are your privacy and security documents?

Can we export our content if we leave?

## How to roll out SOP software in the first 30 days

Start small, with real tasks and one or two locations, and only widen once the routine works. A simple plan:

Days 1 to 7: set up

Choose one owner for the rollout and one or two pilot locations.

Set up locations, roles and who approves.

List the tasks new hires ask about most. Pick the first five to ten.

Days 8 to 14: build

Film or write the first procedures with the people who do the work best.

Review each draft with the expert and approve it with the manager who owns the standard.

Have one new or junior person try each procedure and note where they get stuck.

Days 15 to 21: assign and watch

Assign procedures by role and location in the pilot sites.

Check completion and quiz results every few days. Fix steps behind the questions people miss.

Supervisors keep signing people off on the floor as before.

Days 22 to 30: review and decide

Ask pilot staff and managers what helped and what got in the way.

Agree the update rule: who owns each procedure and when it is reviewed.

Decide the next tasks and locations. Use a training matrix to plan who needs what.

## How Flexlore fits

Flexlore is SOP software for frontline teams, built around video. Available now: film a job on a phone, split it into steps in the phone editor, and let AI draft the instructions and a short quiz that your team edits and approves. Roles, permissions and workspaces by location, and completion and quiz results by person, team and location. iOS and Android apps, with the app in 8 languages.

Coming soon: PDF to steps, screen recording, automatic translation, QR codes on the job, notifications, a web panel for managers, and AI agents and MCP.

Plans are by number of users, from Free up to Enterprise; see pricing. To test it against the checklist above with one of your own tasks, book a demo.

## Questions

**What is the difference between SOP software and an LMS?**
An LMS is built around courses, often long and taken at a desk. SOP software is built around procedures: how a specific task is done, opened on the job and updated when the task changes. Some teams use both. For frontline work, short task procedures with a quick check are usually what people actually use on shift.

**Is there free SOP software?**
Some tools, including Flexlore, offer a free plan for a small number of users. Free plans are useful to test the workflow with real tasks. Check the limits on users, storage, quizzes and AI features, and what happens to your content if you move to a paid plan or leave.

**Can AI write our SOPs?**
AI can draft steps, text and quiz questions from a video or document, which saves time. It cannot know your equipment, your standards or local rules. Treat every AI output as a draft that someone who knows the job reads, corrects and approves before staff see it.

**Does SOP software make us compliant with food safety or safety rules?**
No software makes you compliant by itself. Local rules decide what procedures and records you need, so check them with your authority or advisor. Clear, approved procedures with a record of who was trained can support an audit, but the practice on the floor is what is inspected.

**How long does it take to roll out SOP software?**
A pilot with one or two locations and a handful of real tasks can run within a month if someone owns it. Building a full library takes longer and depends on how many tasks you have and how much time experts can give. Start with the tasks that cause the most questions.

**What should we put in SOP software first?**
Start with the tasks new hires ask about most in their first week, plus any task where a mistake is costly or unsafe. Opening and closing routines, cleaning, machine start-up and changeovers are common first picks. A short list done well beats a large library nobody opens.
